The word spread from Upper German during Middle High German times,gradually displacing the northern `b ōtmuotī (compare from Old Saxon ōthmōdī). derb*{2@^e|Etymology}From a Low German merger of two unrelated adjectives:(1.) from Old Saxon tunleavened,from Proto-Germanic ⋆þerbaz;}and (2.) from Old Saxon coarse,warlike. Both regularly collapsed in ?H tfirm,bold. Older High German had only the former of the two adjectives and lacked the other:£9 tunleavened,`b tunleavened. The modern word is formally High German,but its semantic development has been determined by the Middle Low German one. Drohne*!0Ca. 1600,from gml (variant of commoner ?H drāne),from Old Saxon drāna,é7 ⋆drānu,from Proto-Germanic ⋆drēnuz.}The Low German form replaced older Tren,,£9 tren(e),`b treno,from the Germanic ablaut variant from Proto-Germanic ⋆drenô. This may have been reinforced by the desire to avoid homonymy with Träne. The word was originally a masculine but became feminine in Early Modern German,probably under the influence of Biene. du*Alemannic @0/&_/|Pronoun}#thou,you}German|Alternative forms}Du|Etymology}<4&_,£9 &_o,£9 dū,`b dū (akin to from Old Saxon thū and from English thou),itself é7 ⋆þū,from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆túh₂.é0stressed/&_ː/}:}Ⓓf/ff/De-&_.ogg}:}Ⓓd/d1/De-&_2.ogg}:}Rhymes:uː}unstressed/&_/}unstressed/də/}After the second person singular verb ending -st,the IPAchar:/d/is generally lost when the pronoun is unstressed. Thus  is pronounced IPAchar:ˈhast‿u even in purposefully enunciated speech.}In colloquial speech,chiefly of northern and central Germany,the IPAchar:/d/can be lost after any preceding coronal. Thus  may be pronounced IPAchar:ˈvɛn‿u or IPAchar:ˈvɛn‿ə.|Pronoun}#you (singular familiar),thou|Usage notes}''Du'' is the informal second person pronoun. In formal speech,the third person plural ''Sie'' (always capitalised) is used instead.}A general rule of thumb is that ''&_'' is used to address one's friends,relatives,and those under about 16 years of age. ''Du'' is always used to address children and non-human beings.}Usage also depends on the setting:two unacquainted,middle-aged persons are likely to use ''&_'' when they meet at social gatherings,but much less so when they happen on each other in the street. People under 30 often use ''&_'' among each other,but they still use ''Sie'' when one of them is at work,e.g. in a shop (some cafés and most pubs are an exception).}There is also a great deal of (often subtle) regional variation throughout the German-speaking world.|Derived terms}&_zen}Du||Middle High !0goh,from é7 ⋆þū,from from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū,whence also cog:þū,cog:þú,and ultimately from from Proto-Indo-European ⋆túh₂.|Pronoun}#personal you ''thou'',singular familiar|Inflection}Middle High German personal pronouns|Descendants}Alemannic German:&_}:Swabian:dau,d,(Swabian)}Bavarian:-}:Cimbrian:&_}:Mòcheno:&_}dou}:Hunsrik:&_}:do}German:&_}Luxembourgish:&_}Rhine Franconian:-}:&_}:Pennsylvania German:&_}Yiddish:דו||Middle Low !0From from Old Saxon thū,from from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū.é0/&_ː/|Pronoun}#thou,you Literally:[second person singular nominative]|Descendants}&_,(Low German)||Old High {2thū|Etymology}From é7 ⋆þū,from from Proto-Germanic ⋆þū,whence also cog:þū,cog:þú,and ultimately from from Proto-Indo-European ⋆túh₂. Anders als in Deutschland bedeutet das niederländische Du allerdings keine besondere Nähe,es ist eher mit dem englischen ''you'' zu vergleichen. Im Geschäftskontakt ist es üblich,sich ohne Vorankündigung zu '''@^''',mitten im Gespräch. (...) '''Duzen''' signalisiert nicht,dass man sich in irgendeiner Weise näher gekommen ist,den anderen sympathisch findet oder weniger hart verhandelt. Da gibt es gerade zwischen Deutschen und Niederländern oft Missverständnisse. Wenn etwa ein Vorgesetzter sich '''@^''' lässt,denken Deutsche oft,hier herrsche eine besonders gute Arbeitsatmosphäre – dabei ist das Du einfach eine Anredekonvention.|translationThe fact that Dutch people often come across as relaxed and informal to German people also has to do with the fact that Dutchmen are very quick to '''use the informal form of address''',especially at unexpected moments. Unlike in Germany,however,the Dutch informal you does not imply any particular familiarity; it's more comparable to the English ''you''. In business dealings,it is customary to '''start addressing''' each other '''with the informal you''' without any prior notice,in the middle of a conversation. (...) '''Being on first-name terms''' does not signal that people have become closer in any way,that they find the other person likeable,or that they'll negotiate any less toughly. Especially between Germans and Dutch there often arise misunderstandings in this respect. If,for example,a manager allows himself '''to be addressed using the informal you,''' Germans tend to interpret this as a sign of a particularly good work environment,whereas the informal you is simply a conventional way of addressing people.}#to be on first-name terms|Coordinate terms}erzen}ihrzen}siezen|Derived terms}Duzbruder}Duzen}Duzfreund}Duzfreundin}duzfreundlich}Duzfreundschaft}duzfreundschaftlich}Duzkultur}Duzschwester|See also}de-decl-personal pronouns

-e*@0/ə/,ə,ɘ,(chiefly southern also)e,(Austria also)ɛ|Etymology 1}<4&_,`b -ī,from Proto-Germanic ⋆-į̄.|Suffix}#now chiefly used to form nouns from adjectives,sometimes with umlaut of the root vowel; the nouns express the quality of the adjective}•stark|Etymology 2}<4&_,a merger of various `b - vocalic endings.}Further information on ''&_'' as noun plural suffix}The plural suffix  derives from a merger of `b -a and `b -i. Neuters usually remained unchanged in the nominative and accusative plural. The spread of the suffix to the neuter occurred by analogy with the masculine,whose declension was otherwise identical. Moreover,there were neuters ending in £9 &_ already in the singular; this £9 &_ tended to be apocopated,leading to reinterpretation of the fuller form as the plural (e.g. £9 stücke > modern Stück,pl. Stücke). Another mainly neuter plural suffix is &_r,which see.}Umlaut originally occurred only when the `b - ending had been `b -i,but from the High Middle Ages up to the present there has been a steady trend towards analogical expansion of umlaut in masculines,to the degree that umlautable monosyllables with umlautless plural have become rare (e.g. Hunde,Tage). In feminines,umlaut was seldom expanded,but the umlautless forms have switched to the weak suffix &_n; therefore the ''e''-plural in feminines is now always accompanied by umlaut (excepted are the suffixes -nis and -sal,both of which vary between feminine and neuter gender). Neuters are not umlauted (the only exception being Floß).}{{rel-bottom|Suffix}#used to form the plural of some nouns; in masculines and feminines,but not in neuters,usually triggering umlaut of the root vowel}•Baum}•Nacht}•Wort}#chiefly used to form the dative of strong masculine and neuter nouns ending in a stressed syllable}•''das Haus'' → ''dem Hause'' (usually:''dem Haus'')}#used to form various declined adjective forms,notably the nominative/accusative feminine singular}•schön → ''die schöne Frau''}#used to form the 1st person singular present indicative (and subjunctive) of a verb}•gehen (geh-+&_n) → ''ich gehe'' (colloquial or poetic:''ich geh'')}#used to form the 3rd person singular present subjunctive of a verb}•gehen → ''er gehe''}#used to form the 1st and 3rd person singular past subjunctive of a verb}•ging → ''ich ginge'',''er ginge''|Etymology 3}/d/coalesces with/t/of -st,unstressed/u/weakens to/ə/. (Based on the gender and number of the noun)  the strong declension distinguishes between three forms:the lemma for common gender ''god'' (good)  the t-form for neuter gender ''godt'' (good) and the '''e-form''' for the plural ''gode'' (good).}#}• Steht das Substantiv in der bestimmten Form  benutzen Sie – wie Sie an den Beispielen gesehen haben – die '''@^''' des Adjektivs:den god'''e''' musik ''die gute Musik''  det stor'''e''' bryllup ''die große Hochzeit''  de glad'''e''' gæster ''die frohen Gäste''. (If the noun is in the definite form)  you are to use - as you have seen from the examples - the '''e-form''' of the adjective:den god'''e''' musik ''the good music''  det stor'''e''' bryllup ''the big wedding''  de glad'''e''' gæster ''the happy guests''.}#}• Bei der attributiven Verwendung mit bestimmten Nomen wird unabhängig von Geschlecht und Zahl des Nomens immer die '''@^''' verwendet. einander*£3 @^,`b - compound of ander|nocat1. Semantically limited by the ein to singular contexts,similar to from English one another or from English each other.}The combined form  does not inflect in modern German,and may be used unchanged in dative and accusative grammatical cases. Older forms could show inflection on the second ''ander'' portion,or on both the ''ein'' and ''ander'' portions. Any prepositions,which grammatically and semantically would apply to the second ''ander'' portion of the word,were already appearing in front of the compound term in `b -,and in New High German (i.e.,modern German),prepositions are compounded onto the front of the term.é0/aɪ̯ˈnandɐ/,(standard)}/aɪ̯nˈʔandɐ/,(uncommon and stiff) though etymologically correct}/əˈnandɐ/,(colloquial)}Ⓓ9/91/De-@^.ogg|Pronoun}#each other}•Sie unterstützten '''@^''',so gut sie konnten.}•They supported '''each other''' as much as they could.|Usage notes}Prepositions are prefixed to the pronoun,thus “with each other” becomes '''''mit'''@^''. The spelling ''mit @^'' is not unfrequently seen,but is nonstandard nowadays.}As opposed to English grammar,German ''@^'' is only obligatory after prepositions,or when the reciprocity of the action is not evident from the context:

Einlautung*!0From ein,(in)Laut,(sound)-ung,(-ing).=8linguistics the process by which a word that was borrowed from one language or dialect into a closely related other language/dialect,is adapted to the phonetic system of the latter based not on similarity of sound,but on typical etymological sound correspondences between both varieties|Usage notes}For example,the standard German word echt was first borrowed into the Ripuarian dialect as m:ech. Here the loss of ''-t'' is not a case of  because Ripuarian simply does not allow final ''-t'' after another obstruent. However,the word was then further adapted by way of  in the variant m:ääch,where the lengthening of the vowel follows such pairs as German schlecht,recht vis-à-vis Ripuarian m:schlääch,m:rääch,etc.
